caption: United States v. James Daniel Good Real Property
justification: Clearly controlling SCOTUS case missing from content/cases for the draft Seizure of Property node: absent exigent circumstances, due process requires notice and a meaningful opportunity to be heard before civil-forfeiture seizure of real property; also confirms property forfeiture seizures implicate Fourth and Fifth Amendment protections.

caption: United States v. $8,850 in Currency
justification: Clearly controlling SCOTUS case missing from content/cases for post-seizure property-forfeiture timing: adopts Barker-style four-factor balancing for whether delay between seizure and civil forfeiture filing denies a meaningful hearing at a meaningful time; later reaffirmed by Culley.

caption: United States v. Von Neumann
justification: Clearly controlling SCOTUS case missing from content/cases for seized personal property in forfeiture/remission posture: a timely forfeiture proceeding supplies the required post-seizure due process hearing; remission procedures are not themselves constitutionally required.

caption: Culley v. Marshall
justification: Recent controlling SCOTUS case missing from content/cases and directly on vehicle/property seizures: due process requires a timely forfeiture hearing for seized personal property but not a separate preliminary retention hearing; resolves a circuit conflict and anchors $8,850/Von Neumann in modern civil asset forfeiture.

caption: United States v. Landeros
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
justification: Binding-in-circuit stop-and-identify/traffic-stop candidate missing from content/cases: officers may not prolong a lawful vehicle stop because a passenger refuses to identify himself absent independent reasonable suspicion; fills the draft Stop-and-Identify node and Rodriguez mission-creep edge.

caption: United States v. Black
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
justification: Binding-in-circuit seizure/RAS candidate missing from content/cases: retention of ID while companions are frisked can mark a seizure, and lawful open carry/high-crime-area/association facts did not supply individualized reasonable suspicion; useful for Seizure of the Person, Terry, and Stop-and-Identify edges.

caption: United States v. Robinson
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit (en banc)
justification: Split-marker and binding-in-circuit candidate missing as a standalone case page because content/cases/United States v. Robinson.md is the 1973 SCOTUS SITA case: Fourth Circuit en banc permits a frisk during a lawful traffic stop on reasonable suspicion the occupant is armed, treating danger as flowing from the forced armed encounter; opposite side named by dissent includes 6th/7th Circuits requiring independent dangerousness in lawful-carry settings.

caption: Northrup v. City of Toledo Police Department
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
justification: Split-marker candidate missing from content/cases on the opposite side of the lawful-carry frisk/detention issue: in a legal open-carry jurisdiction, seeing that a person is armed is not enough to stop, disarm, handcuff, or demand ID without facts of criminality or dangerousness; identifies 6th Circuit side against the 4th Circuit Robinson approach.

caption: Noem v. Vasquez Perdomo
justification: Mention-only/adverse frontier item, not a page-candidate: Supreme Court stay order with Kavanaugh concurrence on immigration investigative stops and ethnicity/language/work/location factors. Captured because it bears on reasonable-suspicion seizure doctrine, but interim stay posture and concurrence-only reasoning make it weaker than a merits holding.
